newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-WIMBLEDON GOES SUNDAY-MAD FOR HENMAN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-WIMBLEDON GOES SUNDAY-MAD FOR HENMAN.

text.p: Wimbledon's normally sedate Centre Court erupted like a Cup Final on Sunday as a raucous crowd enjoyed a feast of extra-day tennis including a marathon success for home-boy Tim Henman.

After two washed-out days last week, the All-England Club opened its doors on Sunday's rest day and the fans, many of whom queued all night for cut-price tickets, saw the 14th-seeded Briton beat Paul Haarhuis 6-7 6-3 6-2 4-6 14-12 in six minutes short of four hours.

Football-style chanting accompanied the win, which put two Britons into the fourth round after Greg Rusedski's victory over compatriot Andrew Richardson 6-3 6-4 6-4 on a hardly less noisy new Number One court.
"I've never experienced anything like it before...that noise. It does give you an amazing buzz to have all those people screaming your name," Henman said afterwards.
Only one men's seed fell on Sunday, South African Wayne Ferreira, but six women were blown away, blaming the weather, the grass and bad luck for their misfortune.
Ferreira could not stop Cedric Pioline, the temperamental Frenchman, who can be a match for anyone when on song.

Pioline won 6-4 6-3 6-3 to empty the bottom quarter of the draw of its seeds after the departure of Goran Ivanisevic and Carlos Moya on Saturday and Mark Philippoussis last Monday. The losses have ensured an unseeded semifinalist.
With all the excitement surrounding unusual British success and the women's slump, third and fourth seeds Yevgeny Kafelnikov and defending champion Richard Krajicek slipped through almost unnoticed.

Kafelnikov, last year's French Open champion and a semifinalist earlier this month, took a while to warm to the grass but eventually out-powered Spaniard Javier Sanchez 6-2 4-6 6-3 6-4 in their second round match.
The looming Krajicek hardly broke sweat over his 1.96 metres frame, as he dismissed Czech David Rikl 6-4 6-3 7-5 in the third round. He now meets Henman.

The women fared less well, with fifth seed Lindsay Davenport, sixth seed Amanda Coetzer, seventh seed Anke Huber, former champion Conchita Martinez, seeded 10, number 14 Brenda Schultz-McCarthy and 16 Barbara Paulus all departing.
Olympic champion Davenport said the long wait for her second round match put her badly off her stride as she went down 7-5 6-2 to 18-year-old Czech Denisa Chladkova.
"This week was so weird. I played my first match Monday and to wait to Sunday to play again was a real throw-off," she said.
South African Coetzer, losing 6-2 6-1 to an equally diminutive Patricia Hy Boulais of Canada, said she had not had enough practice on the slippery surface, where the ball went fast and stayed low.
Martinez, brought up on the slow clay of Spain, was served and volleyed out of her match with veteran Czech Helena Sukova 6-4 6-2.

The 1.88 metres Sukova, 32, who has reached the quarter-finals here five times in 16 appearances, has a Wimbledon pedigree as her mother Vera was a finalist here in 1962, but her next match will be fascinating.
Her fourth round opponent is 16-year-old Anna Kournikova who staged another precocious comeback to defeat Huber 3-6 6-4 6-4 in the final singles match of the day.

Schultz-McCarthy earlier lost 6-2 6-3 to Sabine Appelmans of Belgium, who moved better and hit the ball earlier than the tall Dutchwoman. Austria's Paulus went down 5-7 6-3 6-3 to Naoko Kijimuta of Japan.
But Sanchez's sister Aranxta, the eighth seed and finalist here the last two years, did not follow suit. She beat Switzerland's Emmanuelle Gagliardi 6-4 6-2 to advance to the third round.

World number one Martina Hingis sped into the fourth round with a 6-1 6-3 victory over America's Nicole Arendt while Monica Seles won in three sets against Kristina Brandi of the United States without over impressing.
Hingis, the 16-year-old Australian Open champion and runner up in Paris, said she did not feel over-confident.
"You never feel invincible...I don't feel like that at all."
